itineraries.title: Flevoland in 3 Days: Polders, Marker Wadden, and Urk
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, explore Almere’s architecture, the Marker Wadden islands, Urk’s harbor, and the former island of Schokland.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday: Batavialand is closed on Mondays, Museum Nagele is only open Thursday through Sunday, and Urk’s museum is never open on Sundays. The boat to Marker Wadden runs mainly from late March to early November; winter crossings are also available. Book online before you leave.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: in Lelystad, average highs range from 16 to 22 °C, and the boat to Marker Wadden runs during this period. July and August are still the rainiest months, so keep a raincoat handy even in summer. Avoid winter, which is gray and damp with highs of 5 to 7 °C, and days with strong winds along the dikes.

visits.text: White surfaces, glass, and slender steel columns: De Kunstlinie, now called KAF, seems to float weightlessly at the edge of the Weerwater. The Japanese firm SANAA designed and built it between 2000 and 2006; three performance halls rise from an almost square base punctuated by courtyards. If the lobby is open, look for Michael Lin’s large mural, then follow the Esplanade toward The Wave.

Completed in 2005, René van Zuuk’s The Wave undulates above the Weerwater like a swell frozen in place. Its gray-green facade is a reminder that you are walking on a former seabed. Its neighbors, Side by Side and Silverline, complete this waterfront, which grew out of the downtown plan launched in 1994 in the spirit of Rem Koolhaas’s firm OMA. These are residential buildings: admire them from the quay.

The Groene Kathedraal follows the floor plan of Notre-Dame de Reims with 178 Lombardy poplars, planted on April 16, 1987, by artist Marinus Boezem. Measuring about 150 m by 75 m, with trunks around thirty meters tall serving as pillars, this is a nave that grows rather than being built. Nearby, a clearing cut into a young beech grove outlines the same cathedral. Allow 1 hour for both, then head north toward the Oostvaardersplassen.

activities.text: A planned new town, Almere is far from a bland suburb: its first house dates to 1976, and its downtown reads like an architecture catalog. The tourist office’s architecture walk covers a 4.8 km loop in 1 hour 30 minutes, starting at the VVV Almere Citystore. Look up at De Citadel, where Christian de Portzamparc placed homes on the rooftops of stores, then step inside De Nieuwe Bibliotheek, which opened in 2010 and was designed like a department store.

practical_info.tip: Ask for the map at the VVV, Schutterstraat 17, in the pedestrianized center, which also includes Almere Centrum station. Start early to leave the afternoon free for the Oostvaardersplassen.

visits.text: If you only have time for one part of the Oostvaardersplassen, start at the terrace of the Buitencentrum Oostvaardersplassen, at the junction of Kitsweg and Knardijk. Spoonbills and northern shovelers often feed just below. The reserve, created when the polder was drained in 1968, covers about 5,600 hectares, much of it closed to walkers: marked trails start here. The center is closed on Mondays except in July and August.

Forest ranger Hans-Erik Kuypers says that on a fine June day, a reasonably knowledgeable amateur can hear or see around 70 bird species in the Oostvaardersplassen. To take up the challenge, follow Knardijk to the bird blinds at De Kluut, which is accessible to people with limited mobility, and De Grauwe Gans, reached by a path lined with screens. Red deer, Heck cattle, and Konik horses are often seen, and the white-tailed eagle has nested here since 2006.

activities.text: Wear sturdy shoes for the Boswachterspad Roerdomp, a 5.7 km loop marked in orange starting at the Buitencentrum. The trail follows the Keersluisplas to the De Roerdomp observation tower, then a bird blind. The loop and tower close in January and reopen in spring, usually in May. In the Driehoek area, Konik horses are most often seen in summer and fall, frequently accompanied by starlings and cattle egrets. In May and June, listen for bluethroats and reed warblers singing in the reeds.

practical_info.tip: To enter areas closed to independent visitors, book a guided excursion with Staatsbosbeheer in advance. No public transportation serves the Buitencentrum: come by car or bike from Lelystad station.

visits.text: The best time to see Exposure is in the evening, when its steel silhouette stands out against the Markermeer. Antony Gormley used his own body as the model for this crouching man, 26 m tall and weighing 60 tonnes, unveiled on September 17, 2010, on the Markerstrekdam near the Houtrib locks. In an ironic twist, if the dike is raised to cope with rising water levels, the statue could gradually become buried. Arrive before sunset.

From the Ice Age to the present, the Batavialand museum tells the story of the polders and the Zuiderzee coast, with a film showing the landscape 7,000 years ago. The wrecks in the Lost Ships exhibition are a reminder that Lelystad stands on a former seabed. Open Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m., the museum deserves close to two hours; bring a bank card, as cash is not accepted.

activities.text: Next, visit the Batavialand shipyard, where the replica of the Batavia was built between 1985 and 1995 using 17th-century materials and methods. Rope making, nail forging, and wood chiseling are among the workshop activities families can try together. The original ship sank off Australia in 1629. Since October 2, 2026, its replica has been on the museum grounds awaiting restoration: boarding is currently suspended.

practical_info.tip: One ticket covers both the museum and the shipyard. Follow your visit with the early-afternoon boat to Marker Wadden, departing from nearby Bataviahaven.

map_keywords: De Steltloper Observation Tower Marker Wadden

visits.text: The wind whistles at the top of De Steltloper, the observation tower overlooking the entire Marker Wadden archipelago. Below, the De Duikeend bird blind reaches down to water level, with windows for looking beneath the surface, while the Lepelaar bird blind lives up to its name: spoonbills often appear here. Bikes are prohibited, so you explore everything on foot. Save the tower for last, before the return boat.

If a shower threatens, take shelter at the Eilandpaviljoen, the visitor welcome point near the Marker Wadden harbor. Its small exhibition traces the island’s creation and the arrival of wildlife: 193 plant species were recorded in 2021, compared with more than 500 today. Its terrace overlooks the Markermeer, and swimming is allowed at the beach behind the harbor basin.

activities.text: Take the Kustroute instead of the shortcut: this roughly 7 km route follows the shoreline of the island open to the public, passing beaches, mudflats, and bird colonies. Marker Wadden did not exist before 2016, when the first island emerged from sand, clay, and silt dredged from the bottom of the Markermeer. The Netherlands’ first recorded nesting of a long-tailed duck was even documented here. Stay on the paths: the mudflats are dangerous.

practical_info.tip: The Natuurmonumenten boat departs from Lelystad’s Bataviahaven from late March to early November. The round-trip ticket, which must be booked online, gives you a half-day visit of approximately 3 hours 30 minutes on the island, in either the morning or the afternoon.

to_next_leg.road_type: By boat: Marker Wadden → Lelystad → N307 → Urk
to_next_leg.justification: Bateau de visite de Marker Wadden vers Lelystad puis route vers Urk ; pas de liaison régulière directe Marker Wadden–Urk établie.

visits.text: In Urk, she is simply called “Urker vrouw”: a woman facing the sea from which her husband or son should have returned. Unveiled in 1968 by Queen Juliana, the Vissersmonument lists the names of 368 men lost at sea on 34 marble plaques. Rarely has a number carried so much weight in such a small port. Stop by late in the day when arriving from Lelystad, before dinner in the village.

A lighthouse that causes a ship to run aground: this is the most colorful episode in the history of Urk’s Vuurtoren. During World War II, a keeper switched off the emergency lights, and a boat carrying loot, including 226 church bells destined for Germany, ran aground on the De Vormt shoal; the bells were returned after the war. The current tower has shone since 1845, with a Fresnel lens dating from 1876. You can climb it during Dutch school vacations, except on Sundays.

Built in 1904–1905, Urk’s former town hall houses Museum Het Oude Raadhuis and more than a thousand years of local history: traditional clothing, fishing, trade, and art. You can visit a fisherman’s house preserved in its original state, a reminder of the days when Urk was an island. A virtual reality headset takes you down to a Zuiderzee wreck, probably the schokker UK117. Open Monday through Saturday from 11 a.m., never on Sundays.

activities.text: Then stroll through old Urk, an island until 1939, with its unplanned lanes, small squares, and signs on building facades. The Kerkje aan de Zee, the “little church by the sea” completed in 1786, recalls the island days. Look about 30 m offshore for the Ommelebommelestien: according to the legend told to children, this rock is where babies come from.

practical_info.tip: For village stories, book the “Ginkies” tour with a local guide. Listen closely at the harbor: almost all residents speak Urkish, a dialect with more vowels than standard Dutch.

visits.text: Nothing prepares you for the outline of Schokland: a former island 4.5 km long, stranded amid the fields of the Noordoostpolder. The first Dutch site inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, in 1995, Museum Schokland displays footprints more than 4,000 years old, among the oldest in Europe, along with the church dating from 1834. Open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Tuesdays.

activities.text: If you have an extra hour, walk part of the Ruïneroute, a 7.6 km loop starting at Museum Schokland. It crosses the Schokkerbos, passing the ruins of the Ens church and the Zuidert mound, inhabited from the 14th through the 19th century. Here you can appreciate the Schoklanders’ tenacity in the face of the sea, until the evacuation of 1859: around 635 residents were resettled on the mainland, notably in Kampen.

practical_info.tip: Park for free near the De Gesteentetuin visitor center. Some stretches become uneven and muddy after rain; dogs are allowed on a leash.

visits.text: Flat roofs, screens of trees, and a large green heart: Nagele is unlike any other village in the polder. Housed since 1998 in the former Catholic church designed by Taen and Nix, Museum Nagele tells how 33 members of the De 8 architects’ group, from Rietveld to Aldo van Eyck, designed this village between 1947 and 1957. Open Thursday through Sunday, 1 p.m. to 5 p.m.; the Museumkaart is not accepted.

activities.text: Next, explore Nagele with the booklet and map provided at the museum. Seven housing clusters, totaling about 300 homes, surround a shared green space on three sides, sheltered from the polder winds by broad rows of trees. A few streets away, Huis Polman is furnished as it would have been in the 1950s, just after the village was built.

practical_info.tip: The discounted combination ticket covers the museum and Huis Polman. The village homes are occupied: view them from the street.

visits.text: Raw concrete, soft light: at Deltawerk//, in the heart of the Waterloopbos, the walls of the former Deltagoot filter daylight like the slats of a giant blind. This channel generated full-scale waves to test the Delta Works structures. In 2018, RAAAF and Atelier de Lyon cut 80 cm thick slabs and rotated them 90 degrees along a 250 m stretch standing 7 m high. Free access from sunrise to sunset.

activities.text: Beneath its moss, the Waterloopbos conceals more than thirty hydraulic scale models from the former De Voorst laboratory, which operated here from 1951 to 1996. The ports of IJmuiden, Bangkok, and Lagos were tested here in miniature, without pumps: the low-lying terrain alone kept the water flowing. Designated a national monument in 2016, the woods take about 2 hours to explore. In fall, thousands of mushrooms appear: bring boots.

practical_info.tip: There is a parking fee at P1 Waterloopbos for nonmembers of Natuurmonumenten. Paviljoen Het ProefLab serves coffee and lunch daily from 10 a.m.

seo.h1_title: Flevoland in 3 Days: Polders, Marker Wadden, and Urk
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary explores land that was still underwater less than a century ago: Almere’s architecture, the Oostvaardersplassen marshes, and the new islands of Marker Wadden in the south, followed by Urk, Schokland, Nagele, and the Waterloopbos in the Noordoostpolder. One night in Lelystad, two in Urk, and drives of less than 1 hour.
seo.seo_hook: Flevoland in 3 days: Almere’s Groene Kathedraal, the Konik horses of Oostvaardersplassen, the islands of Marker Wadden, and UNESCO-listed Schokland.

Urk: the 1968 Vissersmonument with its 368 engraved names

itineraries.title: Twente in 3 Days: Museums, Gardens, and Medieval Towns
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from Enschede’s museums to the gardens of Diepenheim and Delden, then on to the narrow streets of Ootmarsum.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Thursday: you’ll find Enschede’s synagogue open, followed by the gardens and museums of Diepenheim and Delden on Friday, and the Singraven mill, which can only be visited on Saturday afternoons. Warmelo’s gardens can only be visited from late April to early October, while Twickel’s gardens and Oldenzaal’s basilica are open from April to October.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: in Enschede, average highs range from 18 to 22 °C, and Warmelo’s gardens open from late April to early October, while Twickel’s open from April to October. Bring a rain jacket in every season, as rain falls roughly one day in three. Avoid winter if you’re coming for the gardens: highs range from 3 to 4 °C, and several sites have reduced hours.

visits.text: Few regional museums span as many centuries as the Rijksmuseum Twenthe. Conceived by textile industrialist Jan Bernard van Heek, donated to the state by his widow Edwina, and opened in 1930, it takes you from medieval manuscripts through landscapes by Jacob van Ruisdael and Impressionist paintings to Karel Appel and Armando. Allow 2 hours; it is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Adult admission is €16.50, with free entry for visitors under 18.

The clatter of 19th-century looms, when they are switched on, fills the final room of De Museumfabriek, housed in the former Rozendaal textile factory. Along the way, you’ll encounter a mammoth skeleton and a full-size lös hoes, a Twente farmhouse where family and livestock lived under the same roof. Walk there along Museumlaan from the Rijksmuseum Twenthe; it is closed on Mondays.

Designed by Karel de Bazel for textile manufacturer M. I. Menko, Enschede’s synagogue has stood at the edge of the city center with its three copper domes since 1928. Art Deco meets Eastern influences here, and the building is still used for prayer. Visit on a Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, or Sunday from 11 a.m., never on a Saturday; an audio guide is included in the €7.50 adult ticket, and opening hours are shorter from November to mid-February.

The Grote Kerk stands in the middle of the Oude Markt, surrounded by outdoor café seating. Its Romanesque core, dating to around 1200, was expanded around 1480 into a Gothic hall church, and the fire of 1862 left it with large round-arched windows. Look for the 1836 sundial on the wall; to hear the 1892 Van Dam organ or the 49-bell carillon, check the Wilminktheater’s concert calendar.

Romanesque Revival on paper, almost Byzantine beneath its domes: the Sint-Jacobuskerk, consecrated in 1933, crowns the Oude Markt with twin copper domes. Inside, a Pietà by Mari Andriessen and ceramic Stations of the Cross by Charles Eyck complement the melon-shaped vault. If the door is closed, walk around via Walstraat: the facade on that side looks nothing like the one facing the square.

activities.text: If one neighborhood tells the story of Enschede’s resilience, it is Roombeek. On May 13, 2000, an explosion at the S.E. Fireworks depot killed 23 people and destroyed around 400 homes; architect Pi de Bruijn designed the reconstruction, combining housing, workshops, and cultural spaces around the surviving Rozendaal factory. Explore it on foot between the two museums, with the restraint befitting a place of remembrance.

practical_info.tip: The Rijksmuseum Twenthe and De Museumfabriek border the neighborhood: visit all three on foot during the morning.

activities.text: Stop by the Volkspark on your way back from the synagogue: 15 hectares of lawns and ponds laid out in the 1870s by Dirk Wattez, funded by a bequest from H. J. van Heek. Visit Enschede describes it as the oldest people’s park in the Netherlands. Near the large pond, a sandstone lion has watched over the founder’s memory since 1874, and Mari Andriessen’s war memorial hosts the annual commemoration on May 4.

practical_info.tip: Dogs must be kept on a leash in the park.

visits.text: The gardens at Kasteel Warmelo alone make the detour to Diepenheim worthwhile. Across 7 hectares, a French formal garden, an English landscape park, and a pinetum unfold in succession, dotted with 28 sand sculptures whose theme changes each year. The castle, where Princess Armgard lived from 1952, remains private: the gardens open from late April to early October, Tuesday through Sunday, with admission at €9.50.

“Stedeke,” meaning “little town,” is the locals’ nickname for Diepenheim, home to around 2,600 people. Yet the Drawing Centre Diepenheim gives contemporary drawing a national platform through exhibitions, artist residencies, and works displayed in its garden. Arrive after noon: the center opens Wednesday through Sunday, from noon to 5 p.m.

activities.text: From the Warmelo parking lot, follow the Kastelenroute described by the ANWB to Huize Diepenheim, a residence dating from 1648 whose 180-hectare estate remains open to walkers. Return through the village and Rosarium De Broenshof; the full loop extends to Kasteel Nijenhuis and the Den Haller watermill. Wear suitable footwear: around 40% of the route is unpaved.

practical_info.tip: The Huize Diepenheim manor house and its garden remain private; this route is difficult for strollers and wheelchairs.

visits.text: Around 1830, Jan David Zocher redesigned the park at Kasteel Twickel and had the orangery built there; Hugo Poortman added the surrounding formal garden in the late 19th century, and the last baroness created a rock garden. The castle, still inhabited, opens only a few days a year; the gardens charge admission and can be visited from April to October, Wednesday through Sunday.

Peaceful on the surface, the lands of Twickel conceal a valuable resource underground: salt was discovered here in 1886. In Delden’s historic center, the Zoutmuseum traces this mineral from its discovery through production to its uses today. Save it for late afternoon: it opens only from 2 to 5 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays.

The Oude Blasiuskerk predates Delden: a manuscript mentions it as early as 1119. Construction of its tower began in 1516 but stopped at two levels, and the absence of belfry louvers reveals that a third story was never built. Restoration work between 1965 and 1968 uncovered murals beneath the plaster; ask at the tourist information office about visiting the interior.

activities.text: You can explore Delden’s streets by following Kunststappen, an outdoor art trail whose route description is available at the tourist information office. The town, whose urban history dates back to 1333, also tells its story on a guided walk past its churches, held on Thursdays at 1:30 p.m. from May to October.

practical_info.tip: Pick up the Kunststappen route description at Delden’s tourist information office (VVV) before setting out.

visits.text: Cool stone and scarce light: the north side of the Sint-Plechelmusbasiliek retains the small windows and blind niches of the Romanesque church built around 1180. The treasury holds the silver reliquary of Saint Plechelmus, dated 1480. The church opens only from April to October; its 61-meter tower can be climbed on a guided tour at 2 p.m., Monday through Saturday.

More endearing than a large museum, the Palthe Huis shows how three generations of prominent townspeople lived in the 18th century. A farm building converted into a middle-class residence in the 17th century, it became a museum after Gulia Palthe’s death in 1928 and also houses the town’s collection. Visit Wednesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., on Marktstraat.

activities.text: “Boeskool-stad” is Oldenzaal’s nickname during Carnival, when more than 100,000 people follow the grand parade. During the rest of the year, walk around Marktplein, at the foot of the basilica, to discover the history of a town granted town rights in 1249 and linked to the Hanseatic League through Deventer’s sphere of influence.

practical_info.tip: Oldenzaal station, with connections to Hengelo and Bad Bentheim, is convenient for departing by train the following day.

visits.text: The painting is in London, the mill beside the Dinkel: the National Gallery holds a painting of two watermills by Jacob van Ruisdael from around 1650, believed to depict Singraven. According to the local tourist information office, this is the Netherlands’ only water-powered sawmill. Volunteer millers offer tours on Saturday afternoons from April to October for €2.

Mentioned as early as the late 14th century, Huis Singraven houses furniture, paintings, porcelain, and leather bindings. The residence is managed by the Stichting Edwina van Heek, named after the donor already encountered at the Rijksmuseum Twenthe. Guided tours of the house run from Easter to October, and on Saturday afternoons from November to Easter: buy the Huis, Park & Arboretum ticket at the estate shop.

activities.text: Walk the Singraven route described by the tourist information office, a 6 km loop starting at the mill, following the Dinkel along a bike path, and crossing a 475-hectare estate of woods, meadows, and marshes. The full loop takes around 1 hour 30 minutes; alternatively, allow 1 hour for the paths near the manor house.

practical_info.tip: The estate is open daily from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.; park at the mill, where the De Watermolen restaurant offers a place to take a break.

visits.text: The Openluchtmuseum Ootmarsum brings together sixteen buildings typical of Twente, including farmhouses, barns, a sheep barn, and a forge, to tell the story of rural life a century ago. The Teutonic Order had its commandery here until 1800, and the small mill house is its last surviving vestige. Arrive before 3 p.m.: from February to October, the museum closes at 5 p.m.

“Kunststad van het oosten,” the art town of the East: Ootmarsum’s nickname makes perfect sense at the Museum Ton Schulten. The Twente painter exhibits his vividly colored canvases here, associated with the movement he calls consensism, and one room hosts guest artists. Admission is €7, free for visitors up to age 18; doors open at 11 a.m. Tuesday through Saturday and at noon on Sunday.

As you walk around the Simon en Judaskerk, look to the left of the last window for the black cannonball dated 1597, a reminder of the siege that drove out the Spanish. Built of Bentheim sandstone, the nave dates to around 1230 and features a Westphalian Romanesque-Gothic style rare in the Netherlands. Return at Easter for the poaskearls and vlöggeln rituals in the church forecourt.

activities.text: Start at the Markt, where the Oude Stadhuis, built in 1778, stands beside the pump that, along with three wells, supplied Ootmarsum with water until 1934. The streets still follow the layout of the fortified town, and the Oostwal and Westwal trace the former ramparts. Step into galleries among the half-timbered houses as you make your way to the Cremershuis, built in 1656.

practical_info.tip: Park for free in the Stadsweide parking lot or the open-air museum parking lot.

activities.text: At just seventy-one meters, the Kuiperberg nevertheless offers views over the hedgerow-lined countryside around Ootmarsum. At the summit, an ANWB viewpoint indicator commemorates the festivities of July 1922; the hill also holds the town’s Jewish cemetery, established around 1786. Walk up late in the day, just west of the center, and remain quiet near the graves.

practical_info.tip: The Jewish cemetery is a place for quiet reflection: be respectful and stay on the paths.

seo.h1_title: Twente in 3 Days: Museums, Gardens, and Medieval Towns
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary through Twente starts at the Rijksmuseum Twenthe and Enschede’s synagogue, then heads to the gardens of Kasteel Warmelo and Twickel. It continues to Oldenzaal’s basilica and the Singraven watermill associated with Ruisdael, before an overnight stay among Ootmarsum’s lanes lined with half-timbered houses.
seo.seo_hook: Rijksmuseum Twenthe, the gardens of Warmelo and Twickel, the Singraven watermill, and Ootmarsum’s lanes: 3 days of art and history in Twente.

itineraries.title: Eleven Cities of Friesland in 5 Days, Along the Elfsteden Route
itineraries.subtitle: In 5 days, follow the Elfstedentocht route from Leeuwarden to Dokkum via the ports of the IJsselmeer.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Tuesday: the Fries Museum and Princessehof are closed on Mondays, Museum Dokkum is closed on Sundays, and the Franeker planetarium only accepts advance bookings. From November 1 until spring, the 11Fountains are turned off except for Dokkum’s ice fountain, and several museums reduce their hours.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: in Leeuwarden, average highs range from 16.5 °C in May to 21.6 °C in August. August is also the wettest month, with nearly 94 mm of rain, so keep a rain jacket handy. Avoid November through March if sightseeing is a priority: the Oldehove is closed to climbing, several museums reduce their hours, and the fountains are shut down for the season.

visits.text: A cool mist envelops two 7-meter-tall children’s faces as you leave the station: this is Love, Jaume Plensa’s fountain on Leeuwarden’s Stationsplein. With their eyes closed, they are dreaming, explains the artist, who was inspired by the morning mist over the Frisian meadows. It opens the 11Fountains series, one per city, created for Leeuwarden-Fryslân’s year as European Capital of Culture in 2018. Step into the cloud, about 2 meters high; from November 1 until spring, the fountain is shut down for the season.

Leeuwarden’s most endearing tower is the one that was never finished. Construction of the Oldehove began in 1529, but it started leaning while work was underway and was abandoned in 1533: it stands barely over 39 meters tall, with its top about 2 meters off vertical. You can climb its 183 steps daily from April through the last weekend in October, from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m., for €3.50; cards and cash are accepted.

Set aside 2 hours for the Fries Museum on Wilhelminaplein to understand the province before exploring it. The “Story of Friesland” exhibition traces Frisian history, the fighter Grutte Pier has a place in the collections, and a section follows Mata Hari, born in Leeuwarden in 1876, who became a worldwide media sensation. Temporary exhibitions round out the displays, including one devoted to the legendary King Redbad in 2026–2027. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., with tickets available online.

In 1898, M. C. Escher was born in the city palace that now houses the Keramiekmuseum Princessehof, founded in 1917 by collector Nanne Ottema. The national ceramics museum holds about 35,000 objects, including the Netherlands’ largest collection of Chinese porcelain, imperial pieces, and an overview of Dutch Art Nouveau and Art Deco ceramics from 1880 to 1930. Leave time for Karel Appel’s sculpture; the museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

If a concert is scheduled, step inside the Grote of Jacobijnerkerk to hear its Baroque organ, built by Christian Müller between 1724 and 1727, with 37 stops across three manuals. Begun in 1275 for a Dominican friary, it is Leeuwarden’s oldest building; its choir houses the crypt of the Frisian Nassau family, ransacked in 1795 and restored in 1948. Saint-Saëns and Albert Schweitzer played here. Check the church’s calendar before visiting, as opening hours vary with events.

activities.text: Board Leeuwarden’s canal cruise beneath the orange flag on Willemskade for 1 hour on the canals via the Prinsentuin. On board, the guide projects old photographs, drawings, and paintings onto a large screen, comparing Leeuwarden past and present. The longer cruise, lasting 1 hour 30 minutes, covers all the canals and is known as Leeuwarden’s “8.” Expect to pay €10 for the short cruise and €15 for the long one.

practical_info.tip: Cruise dates are published on the company’s website: check the day’s departures before heading to the orange flag on Willemskade.

visits.text: Sneek is nicknamed “the city of the Waterpoort,” and its water gate, dating from 1613, earns the title with its two octagonal towers. A fun detail: the clock runs five minutes fast, once giving people time to pass through before the gate was locked for the night. On nearby Hoogend, Stephan Balkenhol’s Fortuna fountain depicts a man balancing on a golden ball. Return after dark, when the Waterpoort is illuminated.

The Fries Scheepvaart Museum on Kleinzand explains why Sneek calls itself a city of water: freight and passengers on the canals, skûtsje sailing barge regattas, Sneekweek, and a room devoted to ice skating and the Elfstedentocht. A fine silver collection rounds out the visit. Open daily from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; keep your canal cruise ticket for a discount on admission.

Founded in the 11th century according to Sneek’s tourist office, the Martinikerk was enlarged around 1300 and given a three-towered westwork. Tradition holds that the remains of Grutte Pier, the Frisian fighter who died in 1520, lie within its walls, and its Schnitger organ dates from 1710. The church regularly opens to visitors in summer; during the rest of the year, plan to attend a service or concert.

The most entertaining game at Sneek’s Stadhuis is spotting the symbols hidden in its 1763 Rococo facade, beneath the Baroque entrance steps by sculptor Gerben Jelles Nauta. Built around 1478 on the foundations of two fortified houses, the building has been remodeled many times. Then continue to the statue commemorating the origins of C&A, founded in Sneek in 1841 by Clemens and August Brenninkmeijer.

activities.text: You will duck more than once on Sneek’s historical canal cruise: the bridges are low, which is precisely what allows the small open boat to go where larger vessels cannot. In just under 1 hour, the boat operator tells the city’s story and passes through the Waterpoort. Board at the dock opposite the Fries Scheepvaart Museum ten minutes before departure.

practical_info.tip: Each boat seats no more than eighteen passengers: book through Sneek’s tourist office. The cruise season ends around mid-October.

visits.text: Built in 1711 in the Zaanstreek, the De Rat sawmill was dismantled and transported across the Zuiderzee in 1828 to be installed in IJlst. Logs wait in the Geeuw, the old waterway to Sneek, because wet wood warps less. The mill is open for visits on Saturdays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. year-round, as well as Wednesday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. from May through September. Outside opening days, admire its sails from the Sneekerpad.

Wood shavings, workbenches, and rows of hand planes: the Museum en Werkplaats Houtstad IJlst tells the story of this woodworking city in a workshop that still operates. Jan Nooitgedagt began making planes and chisels here in 1865, and his factory also produced ice skates and wooden toys. Visit in the afternoon, from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. according to the tourist office, and leave with a replica tool.

activities.text: Allow 35 minutes for IJlst’s 2.6 km 11Fountains walk, starting at Shinji Ohmaki’s Immortal Flowers fountain, a black pot filled with stinzen flowers that enters into a dialogue with ikebana. The path follows the gardens on both banks of the Ee, the only ones to have survived intact in the Netherlands according to friesland.nl, then passes the Geeuwbrug and the Nooitgedagt factory chimney.

practical_info.tip: In summer, the fountain stands in a field of flowers near café De Útherne; like the other 11Fountains, it is turned off from November until spring.

to_next_leg.road_type: Overnight in Sneek before continuing to Sloten

visits.text: If it rains in Sloten, head to Museum Sloten, in the former town hall built in 1759–1761 on Heerenwal. Its attic houses a collection of magic lanterns, those projection lanterns of old, which the tourist office calls the finest in the Netherlands. The galleries tell the story of the fortified town, complete with virtual reality headsets. From April through the end of October, it opens Tuesday through Friday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., and on weekend afternoons.

The Lemsterpoort, one of Sloten’s two surviving water gates, has a pillory at its foot: the small town once administered its own justice. Right next door, De Kaai grain mill, built on a bastion in 1755, still grinds wheat. It opens on Saturday afternoons from May through September for tours and flour sales.

activities.text: The best of Sloten fits into 1.4 km: the 11Fountains walking route circles the smallest city in Friesland, whose onion-shaped defenses, designed by Menno van Coehoorn, have retained almost all their ramparts and moats. It starts at Lucy and Jorge Orta’s Peewit fountain, a girl holding a lapwing while sitting on a man’s shoulders, above a pile of buckets and canisters.

practical_info.tip: On Friday evenings in peak season, the town crier gathers the townspeople, and the civic guard fires a cannon near De Kaai mill.

visits.text: In Stavoren, the oldest city in Friesland, people still tell the story of the wealthy widow who had wheat thrown into the harbor: the grain is said to have grown on the sandbar that ruined the town’s trade. Her 1969 statue, the Vrouwtje van Stavoren, gazes out to sea from the old harbor. Then walk along the sea lock dating from 1576, followed by the Johan Friso locks, the second of which was inaugurated by the king in 2014.

Water trickles from the lips of a giant fish 8 meters long: Mark Dion’s De Vis fountain, on Stationsweg near the harbor, was inspired by an engraving by Bruegel the Elder in which big fish eat little ones. It expresses Stavoren’s dependence on the sea, with wealth and danger intertwined. Children play in the spray, except from November until spring, when it is turned off.

You’ll understand the fortunes of this Hanseatic city at Museum ’t Ponthús on Hellingspad: a Viking raid, trade with Hamburg, the Blokhuis fortress, fishing, whaling, the railroad, and the ferry. One room, with a film, explores the legend of the Vrouwtje. Hours vary by season: check with the tourist office before visiting.

Museum Hindeloopen offers the best introduction to this city, a member of the Hanseatic League since 1368. Behind the church, beneath a sculpted figure of Justice above the door, several rooms showcase local dress, Hindeloopen’s brightly colored painting on walls and furniture, and the history of its fishermen, merchants, and harbor. In season, it opens Monday through Saturday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Sunday from noon.

From modest beginnings in 1983, the Fries Schaatsmuseum now claims the world’s largest collection of ice skates. Its Elfsteden room devotes a display case to each winner of the Elfstedentocht, with medals and trophies, while reconstructed workshops depict a forge, a tannery, or a pottery workshop. Allow 1 hour on Kleine Weide: it opens from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Sunday.

activities.text: You can walk around Hindeloopen in 25 minutes on the 1.8 km 11Fountains walking route. It starts at Shen Yuan’s fountain, a tree of life surrounded by a stag and a doe drawn from the coat of arms, where you can sit on giant antlers. It passes the Grote Kerk, whose tower dates from 1593, the 17th-century locks, and the Sylhús with its wooden bell turret.

practical_info.tip: Look for the Kweade Wiif fan Hylpen facade stone at 44 Buren, linked to a local legend.

visits.text: The Jopie Huisman Museum is dedicated to Frisian painter Jopie Huisman (1922–2000), who knew how to find value in humble or discarded objects. In the Golle, the museum café, objects from his home and barn are on display, including his red shirt and milking pants. Open daily from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; admission €12.50, free for ages 12 and under, card payments only.

Twelve painted funeral biers line the side aisles of the Sint-Gertrudiskerk on Merk: nine belonged to guilds, and one was reserved for drowning victims, people who died by suicide, and prostitutes. The tourist office describes it as Friesland’s largest cruciform Late Gothic church, with the largest windows in the province. Look for the rood screen from 1569, then the oldest guild bier, dated 1666.

If boatmen’s stories appeal to you, head up to the attic of Museum Warkums Erfskip, housed in the Waag on Merk: there you can read old letters from boat captain Huijte Fookles. The floors feature models and accounts of Workum’s history, a town linked to Bolsward by a waterway dug in 1620. Allow 30 minutes, then take a look at the former town hall on the same square.

activities.text: Behind the large church, you’ll view Workum through a heart of water formed by the lions from its coat of arms, reimagined with Cornelia Parker’s British humor. Then head to Noard, where merchants’ houses once lined the Wymerts: the Sleeswijckhuis, at number 5, combines a stepped gable with a pilastered gable.

practical_info.tip: Look for the stone inscribed “dit is de workummer peerdestal”: its horse looks toward Bolsward, a reminder of the horse-drawn passenger barges.

visits.text: Four centuries after its construction between 1614 and 1617, Bolsward’s Renaissance Stadhuis became home to the De Tiid center in 2021, inaugurated by King Willem-Alexander. You can visit the wood-paneled council chamber, the restored tower, and an exhibition on Titus Brandsma, who was born near the city and canonized in 2022. Open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Sunday from noon.

The carved choir stalls of the Martinikerk, ranked among the finest in the Netherlands, alone make Bolsward worth a stop. Consecrated in 1459, the church preserves wall paintings from around 1475, a pulpit from 1662 supported by two eagles, and a Hinsz organ with 3,186 pipes, first played in 1781. Ask for opening hours at De Tiid, which houses the tourist office.

A glass roof rests on ruined walls: the Broerekerk, the church of a 13th-century Franciscan friary, burned on May 8, 1980, and remains a roofed ruin. In front, Johan Creten’s dark bat spouts water like a cathedral gargoyle. Climb the steps on its back, as the artwork invites you to do: children can play on it safely.

Harlingen’s Noorderhaven, which became a harbor in 1578, is lined with merchants’ gabled buildings and warehouses named after distant destinations such as Poland, Russia, and Java. The town hall, begun in 1730 by municipal architect H. J. Norel, stands beside the water. From the Prins Hendrik bridge, the view stretches across the inner basins, where the Netherlands’ largest “brown fleet” of traditional sailing vessels is moored.

You will spend more than an hour at the Hannemahuis, a merchant’s house on the Voorstraat whose oldest sections date to the mid-16th century. The museum tells the story of the last whaling ship trapped in the polar ice, genever distillation in 1760, and the rise of Harlingen tiles, including a whaling scene painted around 1770. It opens Wednesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sunday from noon.

Harlingen has produced tin-glazed earthenware and tiles since 1598, and the Harlinger Aardewerk- en Tegelfabriek keeps this craft alive on the Voorstraat, behind a facade covered in its own tiles. Everything is shaped by hand. The shop opens weekdays from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Saturday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.; workshop tours can be booked for groups of more than ten people.

A stranded whale that is still breathing: Allora and Calzadilla’s life-size sperm whale rests near the Zuiderpier, occasionally spouting a one-meter jet of seawater. Harlingen was a whaling port, and the fountain speaks to the human impact on marine life. On the Willemskade, volunteers are rebuilding Willem Barentsz’s expedition ship using traditional methods: the visitor center is open to visitors, while boarding the ship requires an appointment.

If the sky is clear, finish on the Westerzeedijk at the Stenen Man, a monument from 1576 commemorating repairs to the dikes after the All Saints’ Flood of 1570, under Stadtholder Caspar de Robles. From the nearby beach, the view stretches across the Wadden Sea to Terschelling. The dike is exposed to the wind: bring a jacket, even in summer.

The Koninklijk Eise Eisinga Planetarium alone makes the detour to Franeker worthwhile. From 1774 to 1781, wool carder Eise Eisinga installed a solar system on his living room ceiling, driven by a pendulum clock, nine weights, and around 10,000 forged nails, at a scale of one millimeter to one million kilometers. The world’s oldest working planetarium, it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023: admission requires a reserved ticket.

Museum Martena occupies the Martenastins, a fortified residence inhabited since the 16th century. Its university room brings the University of Franeker, active from 1585 to 1811, to life with portraits of professors, one of the three surviving wood libraries in the Netherlands, and a small orrery. One room is dedicated to Anna Maria van Schurman, a 17th-century scholar who corresponded with Descartes. It opens from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday, as well as Mondays from April 1 to October 31.

Twenty-seven colorful coats of arms shine in the stained-glass windows on the second floor of Franeker’s Stadhuis, built from 1591 to 1594 in the Frisian Renaissance style, which partly inspired the Dutch House in Brookline, United States. In the neighboring church garden, Jean-Michel Othoniel’s fountain honors astronomer Jan Hendrik Oort and depicts the birthplace of comets. Twenty minutes is enough for both.

“Hjir rekket de bal it hert,” here the ball touches the heart: the motto of Franeker’s Keatsmuseum sums up the Frisian passion for kaatsen. Opened in 1972, it is the oldest Dutch museum devoted to a single sport, located on the Voorstraat near the Sjûkelân; each year, the PC, a major kaatsen match, returns to Franeker. Check the museum’s website for opening hours before stopping by.

Museum Dokkum is housed in the Admiraliteitshuis, a group of buildings, one of which served the Admiralty of Friesland and Groningen in the 17th century, when it was responsible for protecting the coast. The museum covers two thousand years of northeastern Friesland’s history: silverware, textiles, ceramics, and a permanent exhibition on Boniface in a warehouse dating to around 1800. Open Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed Sunday; admission €7.50.

If you visit between June 1 and September 15, continue to the Bonifatiuskapel on the Bronlaan, open daily from 2 p.m. to 5 p.m., with free admission. It marks the spot where the Anglo-Saxon missionary Boniface was killed on June 5, 754, and welcomes tens of thousands of pilgrims each year. The small park has fourteen Stations of the Cross arranged around the spring.

“Arm Dokkum,” poor Dokkum: the nickname arose when the Stroobos canal diverted traffic away from the Admiralty town. South of the Markt, the Grote Kerk, or Sint-Martinuskerk, stands on a mound and welcomes pilgrims honoring Boniface. Walk around it before heading onto the ramparts: the loop starts close by.

activities.text: You will follow the Dokkumer Bolwerken, former ramparts with six bastions, along the 2.8 km 11Fountains walk, which takes about 40 minutes. Two windmills still operate here, Zeldenrust (1862) and De Hoop (1849), both open to visitors by appointment. The walk starts at Birthe Leemeijer’s ice fountain, a solar-powered copper sculpture with frost that changes every day.

practical_info.tip: The only one of the 11Fountains to operate year-round, the ice fountain is reached via the white footbridge over the Wortelhaven.

visits.text: A prison where people come to read and dine: the Blokhuispoort, a fortress commissioned in 1499 by Stadtholder Willibrord de Schaumburg, served as a prison for around 130 years, until 2007. Today it houses the dBieb library, artisan shops in former cells, the Proefverlof restaurant, and a small free museum. Guided tours led by former guards can be booked online.

activities.text: At dusk, stroll to the Waagplein, where the small Waag was used to weigh butter and other goods from 1598 to 1884, near the statue of a Frisian horse. On Over de Kelders, the statue of Mata Hari commemorates the dancer born in Leeuwarden in 1876. End the evening with a glass of beerenburg, the Frisian herb-infused genever.

practical_info.tip: The Frisian horse statue near the Waag is a popular meeting spot in the heart of Leeuwarden.

seo.h1_title: Eleven Cities of Friesland in 5 Days, Along the Elfsteden Route
seo.intro_paragraph: This 5-day itinerary connects the eleven cities of the Elfstedentocht, the nearly 200 km ice-skating race that starts and ends in Leeuwarden. You travel from the museums of the Frisian capital to the ports of the IJsselmeer, from Sneek to Hindeloopen, then on to Harlingen, Franeker, and Dokkum, before a final evening in Leeuwarden.
seo.seo_hook: Sneek’s Waterpoort, the ports of Hindeloopen and Harlingen, and Franeker’s UNESCO-listed planetarium: Eleven Cities of Friesland in 5 Days, Along the Elfsteden Route.
featured_list: Leeuwarden: the Oldehove, a leaning tower left unfinished since 1533
Sneek: the Waterpoort, built in 1613, and its clock that runs five minutes fast
Hindeloopen: the Fries Schaatsmuseum and its Elfstedentocht room
Franeker: the oldest working planetarium, added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2023
Dokkum: the chapel of Boniface, who was killed near the city in 754

itineraries.title: Utrecht and the Gooi in 3 Days: Canals, Forts, and Castles
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from Utrecht’s wharves and the Rietveld Schröder House to De Haar Castle, Naarden, and Muiderslot.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, or Friday: most museums in Utrecht and Naarden are closed on Mondays, and the Rietveld Schröder House requires a reserved time slot. Naarden’s Grote Kerk is only open for museum visits from the May school break through the fall school break and during the year-end holidays.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: in De Bilt, near Utrecht, average highs rise from 18 °C in May to 23 °C in July. July and August are among the wettest months (around 85 mm): keep a raincoat handy for the ramparts and gardens. From November through March, expect highs of 6 to 10 °C, short days, and winter hours at several sites.

visits.text: Beneath Domplein, it is dark by design: you explore DOMunder with a smart flashlight in hand. In 75 minutes, a guide takes you from the foundations of the Roman fort of Traiectum to medieval remains, ending with the story of the 1674 storm that brought down the cathedral’s nave. Reserve your tour at the information point at Domplein 9: payment is by card only, access is via stairs, and the tour is recommended for ages 8 and up.

The hearts and entrails of two emperors, Conrad II and Henry V, rest beneath the choir of the Domkerk. The choir and transept survive from the Gothic cathedral begun in 1254 and are free to visit; outside, stones in Domplein’s paving outline the nave that collapsed in 1674. Finish at the Pandhof, the cloister garden, open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., whose fountain depicts canon Hugo Wstinc writing. On Saturdays, the church closes at 3:15 p.m.

Climb the 465 steps of the Domtoren, the tallest church tower in the Netherlands at 112 meters, whose exterior restoration was completed in 2024. The climb is only available with a guide and takes about 1 hour, with stops at St. Michael’s Chapel, the Egmond Chapel, and the bell chamber, where the Salvator bell weighs nearly eight tonnes. Leave your bag in a free locker: bags are not allowed in the tower. On clear days, you can make out Amsterdam in the distance.

A scholarly museum, but rarely a quiet one: at Museum Speelklok, carillons, automaton clocks, and street organs play before your eyes. The guides, often conservatory students, operate the instruments themselves inside the Buurkerk, a roughly thousand-year-old church where the recluse Suster Bertken lived for 57 years, walled into a cell measuring less than four meters by four meters. Choose the guided tour over simply wandering through; a combined ticket with the Domtoren is sold on-site, and the museum is closed on Mondays.

If you visit just one Old Master art museum in Utrecht, choose Museum Catharijneconvent. Housed in a medieval convent, it tells the story of Christianity in the Netherlands through paintings by Rembrandt, Saenredam, and Jan van Scorel, manuscripts, and relics, bringing together Catholic and Protestant art. The English audio guide for the permanent collection is free; admission costs 16 euros, or 15 online, payable by card only.

Utrecht is at its most beautiful when seen from below, at water level. Stretching for 4.1 kilometers, the Oudegracht’s wharves, known as werven, serve 732 vaulted cellars dug beneath the street; as early as the second half of the 12th century, tunnels linked the wharves to the cellars of the houses. Head down one of the stairways and walk along the wharf; since 1996, beer boats have continued supplying cafés by water, just as in the Middle Ages.

activities.text: Board a boat for 1 hour on the Oudegracht with Rederij Schuttevaer: from the water, the two levels of wharves and building facades make perfect sense. The route glides beneath old bridges, passes the wharf cellars, and frames views of the Domtoren; a digital guide provides commentary in several languages. Prices start at 18.50 euros; save this trip for late afternoon, after visiting the museums.

practical_info.tip: Departures can be booked online through the company’s calendar; a 1 hour 30 minutes version is also available.

visits.text: The hall at Post Utrecht, on the Neude, was nicknamed the “temple of Posts and Telegraphs.” Completed in 1924 by Joseph Crouwel in the Amsterdam School style, the former main post office now houses the library; beneath the parabolic arches, Hendrik van den Eijnde’s black statues represent the continents. Free admission starting at 9 a.m., 10 a.m. on Sundays.

Small yet revolutionary, the Rietveld Schröder House was built in 1924 by Gerrit Rietveld for Truus Schröder, who lived there until 1985; UNESCO listed it in 2000. Upstairs, sliding and pivoting panels transform the open space into bedrooms. Reserve a time slot, required even with a museum card, and allow 30 to 40 minutes for your visit.

Here, she is called nijntje rather than Miffy, from konijntje, “little rabbit”: the Centraal Museum recreates the studio where Dick Bruna drew for thirty years. Founded in 1838 in a former monastery, the museum claims the world’s largest collection of Rietveld objects and a thousand-year-old boat discovered in 1930. Open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Mondays.

To clear space for his park, Baron Etienne van Zuylen had the village of Haarzuilens moved about one kilometer. De Haar Castle, the largest castle in the Netherlands, was rebuilt starting in 1892 by Pierre Cuypers, at the Rothschild family’s expense, with running water, central heating, and an elevator. Reserve a time slot; last admission is at 4:15 p.m.

activities.text: Allow at least one hour for the gardens of De Haar Castle, open from 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Together with the castle, they cover 45 hectares, where the Roman garden, maze, and Kruisvijver complement one another. Pick up a walking map at reception, then save the late afternoon for the low-angle light on the facades.

practical_info.tip: From early November to early January, hours are reduced: the castle closes at 4 p.m., the gardens at 3:30 p.m. Parking across from the entrance costs 7.50 euros.

visits.text: Even in summer, the chill in the Nederlands Vestingmuseum’s casemates takes you by surprise: the earth covering them maintains a steady temperature. Founded in 1955 by volunteers in the Turfpoort bastion, the museum takes you from underground galleries to cannons, with an exhibition on the water defense lines. Allow at least one hour, Tuesday through Sunday starting at 10:30 a.m.; payment by bank card is required.

Naarden’s Grote Kerk hides its treasure about 25 meters overhead: more than thirty biblical scenes painted between 1510 and 1518 on the oak vault. The tower’s 235 steps lead to a view over the Gooi and the Vecht. Visits are available from the May school break through the fall school break, and at Christmas; admission is 5 euros, 10 with the tower.

Even if the name Comenius means nothing to you, his tomb is intriguing: this Czech educator (1592–1670) rests in the heart of a Dutch fortress. The Comenius Museum traces his life and provides access to the mausoleum, a former convent chapel decorated in the mid-1930s by Czech artists. Visit Tuesday through Sunday, from noon to 5 p.m.

activities.text: Walk around Naarden along its ramparts, ideally on the evening you arrive. Laid out in 1675, the fortress with six bastions and a double moat has been on the World Heritage List since 2021; it is the best preserved of the six fortified towns of the water defense lines. Head back down along Turfpoortstraat: the plaque on the Spaanse Huis commemorates the massacre of 1572.

practical_info.tip: Free parking at the Nieuw Molen bastion parking lot, a short walk from the Grote Kerk.

visits.text: Muiderslot looks like the castle you draw as a child: moats, a drawbridge, and corner towers. Floris V had it built around 1285 and was held captive there before being killed in 1296; the poet P.C. Hooft lived there from 1609 to 1647. Pierre Cuypers, the architect of De Haar Castle, restored it in 1895. The ticket office is open until 4:30 p.m.; a free audio guide is available in English.

activities.text: Since 1673, Muiden’s Groote Zeesluis has had three lock chambers side by side, spanning 50 meters in the center of the small fortified town. Recreational boaters pass through from the Vecht to the IJmeer; across the river mouth stands the Westbatterij, a tower fort dating from 1852. In good weather, choose a terrace beside the lock and watch the boats pass by.

practical_info.tip: Some paths around Muiden are grassy: bring sturdy shoes. From November through March, Muiderslot is closed on Mondays.

activities.text: If night falls early, all the better: the Utrecht Lumen route lights up every evening from sunset to midnight. Stretching 3 kilometers from Domplein, it connects Pausdam, Pieterskerk, Janskerkhof, the Ganzenmarkt tunnel, and the bridges over the Oudegracht, ending at Buurkerkhof, illuminated by Gabriel Lester. Download the map before setting out and take your time.

practical_info.tip: Start at the information point at Domplein 9; the route map can be downloaded from the tourist office’s website.

activities.text: Head downstairs for dinner in a werfkelder on the Oudegracht, one of the vaulted cellars beneath the street that have become cafés and restaurants. In the 19th century, some even served as homes; the tourist office recommends their indoor dining rooms in winter and tables on the wharves in summer. Reserve, especially on weekends, and request a table by the water if the weather allows.

practical_info.tip: In dry weather, tables on the wharves fill up quickly: reserve in the afternoon.

seo.intro_paragraph: Over 3 days, this itinerary devotes a day and a half to Utrecht, from the Domtoren to the cellars of the Oudegracht and the UNESCO-listed Rietveld Schröder House. It then heads to De Haar Castle, includes an overnight stay in the fortress town of Naarden, and stops at Muiderslot before a final evening of lights in Utrecht.
